name: Raw honey / bee pollen
lead: Raw honey is honey taken from the hive and extracted, settled or strained without added heat, so it may retain some pollen and wax particles.[1] Bee pollen is the ball of flower pollen that worker honeybees pack and use as the hive's main food, mixed with nectar and salivary secretions.[2] People in wellness and looksmaxxing circles use raw honey as a face wash, mask or scrub and as a food for smoother, softer, more even-looking skin, and take bee pollen as a supplement for energy and general nutrition that supports training and appearance.[3][4]

Honey is mostly fructose and glucose, with a pH averaging about 3.9, and is reported to have broad antibacterial activity.[1] Bee pollen composition is variable, with about 40 to 60 percent simple sugars and 20 to 60 percent protein by one estimate.[2] Looksmax.org members describe honey as a humectant, meaning it draws water into the skin surface.[3]

For honey, Wikipedia reports preliminary evidence of faster healing of partial-thickness burns and moderate evidence for some post-operative wounds, with lower-quality evidence for other uses.[1] A 2020 review of bee products in dermatology describes honey, propolis and pollen as used for burn wounds and as having antibacterial, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, and suggests bee products could be ingredients in skin medicines and cosmetics.[5] No published trial was found testing either product for the appearance of healthy skin or for testosterone.

chain: Honey applied as a wash, mask or scrub

angle.text: Users apply raw or mānuka honey to the face as a wash or mask for softness and hydration, and some take bee pollen as a nutrient-dense food. The skin benefit people report is a soft, moisturized feel after rinsing.

infobox: Mostly fructose and glucose, about 15.5 to 18% water[1]
Variable; roughly 40 to 60% sugars, 20 to 60% protein[2]

paras: Honey is a supersaturated sugar solution whose high sugar content and acidity keep most microbes from growing. Raw honey is not heated, whereas pasteurisation at 72 C or higher destroys yeast but can increase hydroxymethylfurfural and reduce enzyme activity.[1]

Wikipedia reports preliminary evidence that honey helps partial-thickness burns heal 4 to 5 days faster than other dressings, and moderate evidence for faster healing of post-operative infections. Evidence for other wounds is low quality, and the FDA has approved some medical-grade honey products for minor wounds and burns.[1] A Cochrane review found no strong evidence for or against honey for cough, and evidence for allergy relief is inconclusive.[1]

Infants can develop botulism from honey containing Clostridium botulinum spores, and honey is not recommended before age one.[1] Honey is also sometimes adulterated with corn syrup or other sugars, and no single method detects all forms of adulteration.[1]

Mānuka honey is made from the nectar of the mānuka tree (Leptospermum scoparium) of New Zealand and Australia. It is graded by methylglyoxal content (MGO) and the Unique Mānuka Factor (UMF), and its marker compounds are used to authenticate it. Traditional Māori medicine used mānuka leaf and bark preparations for colds and for wounds and skin conditions.[6] Wikipedia notes that UK government tests in 2011 to 2013 found many mānuka-labelled honeys lacked mānuka-specific activity, and that the US FDA issued warning letters between 2022 and 2025 to manufacturers over eye-therapy and anti-allergy claims.[6] The article does not cite clinical trials on skincare use.[6]

Bee pollen's composition varies with the plants foragers visit and with time and location, so no two samples are identical.[2] Wikipedia describes the health benefits marketed for it as yet unproven.[2]

It is considered safe for short-term use by most people, but people with pollen allergies may experience shortness of breath, hives, swelling or anaphylaxis, and contamination by mycotoxins, pesticides or toxic metals is a risk. It is not considered safe in pregnancy and should be avoided while breastfeeding.[2] The FDA warned consumers about certain bee pollen products, including a Zi Xiu Tang capsule product in 2012 and 2014, because they were adulterated with unapproved drugs sibutramine and phenolphthalein.[2]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: A looksmax.org thread describes washing the face with manuka honey twice daily, using raw honey as a mask nightly and as a scrub several times a week, and reports softer skin than with other products.[3] Other members in the thread called honey a good humectant but not a cure-all and cautioned against scrubbing the face frequently.[3]

On T Nation, bee pollen and raw honey appear in members' diet logs, for example raw honey mixed with bee pollen at breakfast, and in a thread where a member argues raw honey keeps benefits that processed honey loses.[7][8] Wikipedia's honey article covers skin only in relation to wounds and burns and does not report evidence for testosterone effects.[1]

No studies found on raw honey or bee pollen for the appearance of healthy skin or for testosterone. Related clinical research includes a 2025 randomized trial of raw honey dressings versus saline for leprosy foot ulcers in Nigeria (130 participants), which found complete healing in 29.2 percent of honey-treated ulcers versus 24.6 percent with saline, a difference that was not statistically significant, with no treatment-related adverse events.[9] Reviews of bee products in dermatology and as apitherapy summarize laboratory and clinical findings on wound healing and antimicrobial activity.[5][10]

timeline.event: FDA issues a notice about a bee pollen capsule product adulterated with unapproved drugs; a further notice follows in 2014.[2]
New Zealand's science definition test for mānuka honey takes effect on 5 January.[6]
Randomized trial of raw honey dressings for leprosy ulcers published.[9]

lore.intro: Honey is discussed on looksmax.org as a skin product and on T Nation as a food and supplement ingredient.[3][7][8]

claims.claim: Washing and masking the face with raw or manuka honey gives better skin
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says nightly masks, scrubs several times a week and washing with manuka honey left skin soft and never dry.[3]
claims.experts: Forum members call honey a humectant, and a 2020 review lists antibacterial, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties of bee products; no trial was found testing honey masks on healthy skin appearance.[5]

claims.claim: Raw honey keeps benefits that processed honey loses
claims.believers: A T Nation member says regular squeeze-bottle honey is heavily processed and lacks benefits of raw honey, such as the bee pollen that sits on top.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes pasteurisation can reduce enzyme activity and raise hydroxymethylfurfural; it does not report health-outcome differences between raw and processed honey.[1]

claims.claim: Bee pollen provides energy and general health benefits
claims.believers: Some T Nation members include bee pollen with raw honey in their diets.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the marketed health benefits of bee pollen as unproven and lists allergy risk and contamination concerns.[2]

card.summary: Hive products promoted for skin and testosterone; honey has some wound-care evidence, bee pollen's benefits are described as unproven.
card.aka: Raw honey, unpasteurised honey, bee bread
card.note: Bee pollen can trigger allergic reactions including anaphylaxis; honey is not recommended for infants under one year.

quick.overview:
Raw honey is honey that has not been heated or pasteurised, and bee pollen is the pollen pellets bees collect and store as food. In wellness and looksmaxxing circles both are promoted for skin, energy and testosterone.

Honey has preliminary evidence for some wound and burn dressings but none for appearance or hormones, and Wikipedia describes bee pollen's health benefits as unproven. No published trial was found testing either for skin appearance or testosterone in healthy people.
quick.mechanism: Honey is mostly fructose and glucose with some acids and aromatic compounds, and has antibacterial activity that varies between honeys. Bee pollen is a variable mix of sugars, protein, minerals, vitamins and fatty acids. How either would change skin or hormones has not been shown.
quick.risks: Bee pollen can cause allergic reactions in people allergic to pollen, ranging from hives to anaphylaxis, and may be contaminated with mycotoxins, pesticides or metals; it is not considered safe in pregnancy. Honey can carry Clostridium botulinum spores and is not recommended for infants under one year. The FDA has warned about bee pollen products adulterated with unapproved drugs.
